lexemes.note: To wake up (by oneself). Hitpa‘el: past הִתְעוֹרַרְתִּי, present מִתְעוֹרֵר, future יִתְעוֹרֵר, infinitive לְהִתְעוֹרֵר. Waking someone else is הֵעִיר.

profile.feeling: The first moment of the day: the alarm rings, the eyes open.

senses.def: to wake up (from sleep, by oneself)
to come to life, stir (a city, nature, interest)

examples.tr: I woke up at six in the morning.
The baby woke up in the night.
When do you (m.) usually wake up?
The city slowly comes to life.

collocations.tr: alarm clock (“a waking clock”, the same root in pi‘el)

synonyms.nuance: “to get up” — out of bed; הִתְעוֹרֵר is only opening one’s eyes

etymology.text: Hitpa‘el of the root ע־ו־ר “awake” (Wiktionary gives no further etymology). From the same root: עֵר “awake” and the causative הֵעִיר “to wake (someone)”, which Wiktionary lists for “to awaken (someone else)”.

funFacts: An alarm clock is a שָׁעוֹן מְעוֹרֵר, literally “a waking clock” — the same root.
pitfalls: הִתְעוֹרֵר is waking up yourself. Waking someone else is הֵעִיר: הִיא הֵעִירָה אוֹתִי “she woke me up”.
The ר is written twice where an ending follows: הִתְעוֹרְרָה, מִתְעוֹרְרִים, הִתְעוֹרַרְתִּי.
subtleties: Past and present differ in the first letter only: הִתְעוֹרֵר “he woke up” — מִתְעוֹרֵר “he wakes up”.
No object and no reflexive pronoun: the hitpa‘el form already says that it happens to the subject.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: To get up, rise. A hollow root (ק־ו־ם): past קַמְתִּי, present קָם / קָמָה, future יָקוּם, imperative קוּם!, infinitive לָקוּם.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses קָם as “to rise, stand up”, without the words of the course gloss “to get up”; rising from bed is its everyday use (קַמְתִּי בְּשֶׁבַע).

profile.feeling: Feet on the floor: getting out of bed, standing up from a chair.

senses.def: to get up (out of bed), rise
to stand up (from a seat), with מִ “from”

examples.tr: I got up at seven and went to work.
On Saturday I (m.) get up late.
Get up! It’s already eight!
Everyone stood up when the teacher came in.

phrases.tr: got up on the left side
phrases.meaning: got out of bed on the wrong side; is in a bad mood

synonyms.nuance: “to wake up” — the eyes open; קָם is getting out of bed
“to get up early” — written style (הִשְׁכִּים קוּם)

etymology.text: Common Semitic; compare Arabic قَامَ (qāma) and Ge’ez ቆመ (ḳomä) (Wiktionary). From the same root: קִימָה “getting up” and מָקוֹם “place”.

funFacts: מָקוֹם “place” comes from the same root: the place where one stands.
pitfalls: In the masculine singular the past and the present are the same word: קָם “got up” and “gets up”. The feminine קָמָה too — the past is stressed on the first syllable (KA-ma), the present on the last (ka-MA).
A hollow root: only two letters show in the past and present (קַמְתִּי, קָמִים); the ו comes back in the future, the imperative and the infinitive: יָקוּם, קוּם!, לָקוּם.
subtleties: In formal style קָם also means “came into being, was founded”: קָמָה מְדִינָה “a state was founded”.
The pronoun can be dropped in the 1st and 2nd person of the past: קַמְתִּי “I got up” — the ending says who.

lexemes.note: To wash (the body, hands, face; someone). Pa‘al; the future has a (יִרְחַץ) because of the ח; infinitive לִרְחֹץ (full spelling לרחוץ). Clothes: כִּבֵּס; dishes: usually שָׁטַף.

profile.feeling: Water and soap: a face in the morning, hands before a meal.

senses.def: to wash (the body, the face, the hands; someone; also things, in careful speech)

examples.tr: I washed my face and brushed my teeth.
Wash your hands before the meal!
She is bathing the baby.

collocations.tr: a bathing beach (the noun of the same root)

synonyms.nuance: “to rinse, wash with running water” — dishes, the floor, a car (שָׁטַף כֵּלִים)
“to wash clothes, do the laundry” (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)
“to wash oneself, bathe” — the reflexive, with no object

etymology.text: From the root ר־ח־ץ (Wiktionary gives no etymology). From the same root: רְחִיצָה “washing” (the verbal noun, Wiktionary) and רַחְצָה “bathing”.

funFacts: A beach with lifeguards is a חוֹף רַחְצָה, a “bathing beach” — the same root.
pitfalls: Body parts are a bare object, often without the article and without “my”: רָחַצְתִּי יָדַיִם “I washed my hands”.
Clothes are not רָחַץ but כִּבֵּס: כִּבַּסְתִּי בְּגָדִים “I did the laundry”.
The ח takes a hataf vowel before an ending: רָחֲצָה, רוֹחֲצִים; and the future has a: יִרְחַץ.
subtleties: In everyday speech dishes and floors are more often שָׁטַף; רָחַץ is above all washing the body.

lexemes.note: To take a shower. Hitpa‘el with a final ח: past הִתְקַלַּחְתִּי, present מִתְקַלֵּחַ / מִתְקַלַּחַת, infinitive לְהִתְקַלֵּחַ.

profile.feeling: Hot water after a long day, or a quick cold one in the summer heat.

examples.tr: I showered and got dressed.
I (m.) shower every evening.
She showers after her run.

collocations.tr: a cold shower (the noun of the same root)

synonyms.nuance: “had (did) a shower” — with the noun מִקְלַחַת
“to wash oneself, bathe” — in a bath, in the sea; not specifically a shower

etymology.text: Hitpa‘el of the root ק־ל־ח (Wiktionary gives no further etymology); the noun מִקְלַחַת “shower” is from the same root.

funFacts: מִקְלַחַת is both the act (“a shower”) and the place (“the shower”): אֲנִי בַּמִּקְלַחַת “I’m in the shower”.
pitfalls: The final ח takes a furtive patach: הִתְקַלֵּחַ is said hitkaléach; before the feminine ending the vowels change: מִתְקַלַּחַת.
Hitpa‘el, but it takes no object and no “oneself”: just הִתְקַלַּחְתִּי “I showered”.
subtleties: The future keeps the e and the furtive patach (Wiktionary): יִתְקַלֵּחַ, תִּתְקַלֵּחַ.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: To get dressed. Hitpa‘el of ל־ב־שׁ; putting on one garment is לָבַשׁ + the garment.

profile.feeling: Choosing clothes in the morning, children struggling with their sleeves.

senses.def: to dress (in a certain way): הִתְלַבֵּשׁ יָפֶה “dress nicely”

examples.tr: I got dressed quickly and went out.
The children get dressed by themselves.
She always dresses nicely.

synonyms.nuance: “to put on, wear (a garment)” — with an object: לָבַשׁ מְעִיל; הִתְלַבֵּשׁ has none

etymology.text: Reflexive (hitpa‘el) of לָבַשׁ “to dress, put on” (Wiktionary). From the same root: לְבוּשׁ “clothing”.

funFacts: The whole family of clothes words: לָבַשׁ “put on”, הִתְלַבֵּשׁ “get dressed”, הִלְבִּישׁ “dress (someone)”, לְבוּשׁ “clothing”.
pitfalls: No object: “I put on a coat” is לָבַשְׁתִּי מְעִיל, not הִתְלַבַּשְׁתִּי מְעִיל.
Dressing a child is the causative הִלְבִּישׁ: הִיא הִלְבִּישָׁה אֶת הַיֶּלֶד.
subtleties: In slang הִתְלַבֵּשׁ עַל means “to latch onto, go after (someone or something)”.

meaningForms.none: the same forms in every meaning

lexemes.note: To start, begin. Hif‘il: past הִתְחִיל / הִתְחַלְתִּי, present מַתְחִיל, future יַתְחִיל, infinitive לְהַתְחִיל. + infinitive for “start doing”.

profile.feeling: The bell rings, the film begins, a new job on Sunday morning.

senses.def: to start, begin (something; to do something: + infinitive)
to begin, start (without an object: the lesson starts)

examples.tr: I started learning Hebrew a year ago.

examples.text: הוּא הִתְחִיל אֶת הַיּוֹם עִם קָפֶה.
examples.tr: He started the day with a coffee.
Work starts at nine.
When does the lesson start?

synonyms.nuance: “to open, start” — a meeting, a speech, a season (פָּתַח אֶת הַיְּשִׁיבָה)
“to begin, commence” — written and official style

etymology.text: Hif‘il of the root ת־ח־ל (Wiktionary gives no etymology); the verbal noun is הַתְחָלָה “beginning” (Wiktionary), and the same root gives the formal תְּחִלָּה “beginning”.

funFacts: “In the beginning” of the Bible is בְּרֵאשִׁית, another root — today a beginning is a הַתְחָלָה.
pitfalls: The present starts with מַ־ (hif‘il): מַתְחִיל, מַתְחִילָה — not מִתְחִיל.
To start doing something: הִתְחִיל + infinitive (הִתְחַלְתִּי לִלְמֹד); a definite object takes אֶת (הִתְחִיל אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה).
In the past the i becomes a before an ending of the 1st or 2nd person: הִתְחִיל but הִתְחַלְתִּי, הִתְחַלְנוּ.
subtleties: Colloquially הִתְחִיל עִם means “to hit on, make a move on (someone)” (Wiktionary).
Without an object it is “to begin” of events: הַסֶּרֶט מַתְחִיל “the film is starting”.

lexemes.note: To finish. Pi‘el of ס־י־ם with a consonantal י (written double: סיים): past סִיַּמְתִּי, present מְסַיֵּם, future יְסַיֵּם, infinitive לְסַיֵּם. Colloquial synonym: גָּמַר.

profile.feeling: The end of the working day, the last page of a book, a diploma.

senses.def: to finish, complete (something; doing something: + infinitive)

examples.tr: I finished work at five.
When do you (m.) finish today?

examples.text: הִיא סִיְּמָה אֶת הַסֵּפֶר בְּלַיְלָה אֶחָד.
examples.tr: She finished the book in one night.

examples.text: הוּא סִיֵּם אֶת הַלִּמּוּדִים לִפְנֵי שְׁנָתַיִם.
examples.tr: He finished his studies two years ago.

synonyms.nuance: “to finish” — the everyday word in speech (גָּמַרְתִּי!), but it also has a vulgar sense (Wiktionary)
“to complete” — a task, a project, a gap

etymology.text: Pi‘el of the root ס־י־ם (Wiktionary gives no etymology); the verbal noun is סִיּוּם “end, completion” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: A סִיּוּם is also the festive meal for finishing the study of a tractate of the Talmud.
pitfalls: The י is a consonant and is doubled: סִיַּמְתִּי, מְסַיֵּם — in everyday spelling with two yods: סיימתי, מסיים.
גָּמַר is just as common in speech, but it is also a vulgar word (Wiktionary): סִיֵּם is the safe choice in writing and with strangers.
Finishing doing something takes the infinitive: סִיַּמְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל “I finished eating”.
subtleties: As in all pi‘el verbs the present starts with מְ־: מְסַיֵּם, מְסַיֶּמֶת.

lexemes.note: To fall asleep. Nif‘al: past נִרְדַּמְתִּי, present נִרְדָּם, future יֵרָדֵם, infinitive לְהֵרָדֵם (full spelling להירדם). Being asleep: יָשֵׁן.

profile.feeling: Eyes closing in front of the television; a baby finally quiet.

examples.tr: I fell asleep in front of the TV.
The baby finally fell asleep.
It’s hard for me to fall asleep at night.

synonyms.nuance: “to doze, nod off” — a short light sleep

etymology.text: Nif‘al of the root ר־ד־ם (Wiktionary); the first sense in Wiktionary is “to sleep deeply”. From the same root: תַּרְדֵּמָה “deep sleep” — the sleep that falls on Adam in Genesis 2:21.

funFacts: Anaesthesia is הַרְדָּמָה, “putting into deep sleep” — the same root.
pitfalls: Falling asleep is נִרְדַּם; being asleep is יָשֵׁן: הוּא נִרְדַּם בְּעֶשֶׂר וְיָשַׁן עַד שֶׁבַע.
The ר takes no dagesh, so the future and the infinitive have e under the prefix: תֵּרָדֵם, לְהֵרָדֵם (everyday spelling תירדם, להירדם).
subtleties: Of a limb, נִרְדַּם is “went numb, fell asleep”: הָרֶגֶל שֶׁלִּי נִרְדְּמָה “my leg has gone to sleep”.

lexemes.note: To sleep, be asleep. Pa‘al with a first י and a stative present: יָשֵׁן / יְשֵׁנָה; past יָשַׁנְתִּי, future יִישַׁן, infinitive לִישֹׁן (full spelling לישון). Do not confuse with the adjective יָשָׁן “old”.

profile.feeling: Night, a dark room, a quiet house; “sleep well!”.

examples.tr: I slept eight hours.
The children are asleep.
Good night, sleep well!

synonyms.nuance: “to slumber” (Wiktionary lists it as a synonym)

etymology.text: From the root י־שׁ־ן (Wiktionary gives no etymology); its verbal noun is שֵׁנָה “sleep” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: “Going to bed” has no verb of its own: it is הָלַךְ לִישֹׁן, “went to sleep”.
pitfalls: Three words, one spelling: unvocalized ישן is יָשַׁן “slept”, יָשֵׁן “sleeps, is asleep” and the adjective יָשָׁן “old” (lesson 16).
In the 1st person plural the נ of the root and of the ending merge: יָשַׁנּוּ “we slept”.
The infinitive is לִישֹׁן (full spelling לישון), and the future keeps the י as a vowel letter: יִישַׁן, תִּישַׁן.
subtleties: The present יָשֵׁן, יְשֵׁנָה is also a state: הוּא יָשֵׁן “he is asleep”.

absent.reason: Hebrew has no verb “to breakfast” in everyday use: the meal is eaten with the ordinary verb “to eat”.
absent.use: אָכַל אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר “ate breakfast” (אָכַלְתִּי אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר, both words from lesson 7); formal סָעַד אֲרוּחַת בֹּקֶר.

absent.reason: No single verb: leaving home is the verb “to go out” with “from the house”.
absent.use: יָצָא מֵהַבַּיִת (lesson 13: יָצָאתִי מֵהַבַּיִת בִּשְׁמוֹנֶה “I left home at eight”).

absent.reason: No single verb: coming home is “to return” or “to arrive” with the direction word הַבַּיְתָה “home(wards)”.
absent.use: חָזַר הַבַּיְתָה “came back home”, הִגִּיעַ הַבַּיְתָה “got home” (lessons 11 and 13).

absent.reason: No single verb: going to bed is “going to sleep”.
absent.use: הָלַךְ לִישֹׁן (הָלַךְ + the infinitive of יָשַׁן): הָלַכְתִּי לִישֹׁן בְּאַחַת עֶשְׂרֵה “I went to bed at eleven”; also נִכְנַס לַמִּטָּה “got into bed”.
